extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, judges, and other patent-law practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and construing patent claim terms for indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. § 112 ¶ 2 on appeal, using intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history) and limited extrinsic evidence. Focuses on when amendments and prosecution statements clarify claim scope and when multiple plausible interpretations do not render a claim indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness requirement (Nautilus reasonable-certainty standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 112 requires that 'a patent’s claims, viewed in light of the specification and prosecution history, inform those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention with reasonable certainty.' The court must ensure claims do not create an 'innovation-discouraging "zone of uncertainty."' (citing Nautilus, Inc. v. Biosig Instruments, Inc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a skilled artisan, in view of the intrinsic record, can determine claim scope with reasonable certainty. Look for a 'zone of uncertainty' that would make the claim invalid; if the intrinsic evidence provides reasonable certainty, the claim is not indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-construction sources and hierarchy (Phillips)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret claims by looking to the claim language, the specification, the prosecution history, and, where relevant, extrinsic evidence. 'The prosecution history, in particular, may be critical in interpreting disputed claim terms.' (Phillips v. AWH Corp. and Personalized Media communications citation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with claim language; consult specification for context; use prosecution history to resolve ambiguities; use extrinsic evidence only when relevant and subordinate to intrinsic record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution-history amendments can define/limit claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment made to overcome a prior-art rejection can be used to construe disputed claim language. The circumstances of an amendment that overcame a prior-art rejection can provide sufficient clarity to construe a limitation. (Citing example where amendment distinguishing Hirshberg informed the meaning of 'only one option').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim was amended to overcome a reference, interpret the amended language in light of the rationale for the amendment. Such amendments may limit the number of permissible constructions if they were made to avoid prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot establish indefiniteness merely by identifying multiple plausible interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: A party cannot show indefiniteness by 'merely identify[ing] different ways one could interpret' a claim term; otherwise nearly every term could be found indefinite. (Citing ClearOne, Nevro).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove indefiniteness the challenger must show that, after considering the intrinsic record, reasonable certainty is lacking. If the intrinsic evidence resolves among competing interpretations, indefiniteness is not established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic record controls; embodiments inform but do not necessarily limit
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification’s embodiments help interpret claim scope but do not automatically limit claims to those embodiments. The intrinsic record—claims, specification, prosecution history—resolves meanings; reliance on one embodiment alone does not necessarily restrict claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use embodiments to illuminate meaning, but avoid importing unnecessary limitations from a preferred embodiment into the claim unless the intrinsic record requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate legal conclusion of indefiniteness and any determinations based on intrinsic evidence are reviewed de novo; underlying factual determinations are reviewed for clear error. (Cox Commc’ns, Inc. v. Sprint Commc’n Co.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On appeal, accept district court’s factual findings unless clearly erroneous; review claim-construction and indefiniteness conclusions anew.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to construe 'wherein the representation consists of only one option for activating the function'
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpreted (on this record) as 'wherein the representation consists of only one option for what function to activate at a given time (where a given time means the currently active application).' The 'option' limits how many functions can be activated from a given representation to one, though that single function can change depending on the active application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the limitation was added to distinguish prior art (e.g., Hirshberg's multifunction keys). Treat 'option' as referring to number of functions activatable from a representation (not the gesture itself). Consider specification language (e.g., claim 2 and embodiments) and prosecution statements that overcame the prior-art rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of isolated or inconsistent prosecution/litigation statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated or contextless statements (e.g., post-allowance remarks or snippets from IPRs/litigation) do not necessarily change a claim construction or render a claim indefinite. The intrinsic record must be read as a whole; a 'bare statement made after allowance' is insufficient to override the rest of the prosecution history and specification. (Citing Univ. of Mass. v. L’Oréal and Sequoia Tech. v. Dell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh inconsistent or imprecise statements in the full context of prosecution and specification. Do not elevate isolated remarks above the broader intrinsic record that indicates meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating terms susceptible to plain-and-ordinary-meaning construction ('gliding . . . away')
rubrics_metrics.description: A term may be given its plain and ordinary meaning so long as that meaning, read in the context of the claim and intrinsic record, provides reasonable certainty and excludes clearly distinguishable operations (here, the court endorsed a plain-and-ordinary-meaning construction of 'gliding . . . away' with the caveat it 'did not include dragging, flicking, or a drag and drop operation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plain and ordinary meaning, together with intrinsic evidence and prosecution history, imparts reasonable certainty to a skilled artisan, that construction is acceptable. Compare prior decisions (e.g., companion Google v. Neonode) for consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using amendments to distinguish prior art and thereby narrow claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim amendment is made expressly 'in distinction' to a prior-art reference, that amendment can be understood to limit claim scope in the way necessary to avoid the reference (e.g., adding 'only one option' to distinguish Hirshberg’s multifunction keys).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat narrowing amendments as evidence the patentee surrendered certain claim scope during prosecution; incorporate that surrendered meaning into claim construction where appropriate to preserve consistency with prosecution history.
